messages.content: Could you retrieve the current weather data for New York, specifically focusing on the temperature?.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

The user wants current weather data for New York, focusing on temperature. We need to use the tool `requests_get` to fetch data from Open-Meteo API.

We have to provide the correct query parameters:

Open-Meteo API requires latitude and longitude. For New York City, approximate coordinates: lat=40.7128, lon=-74.0060.

Also we want "current_weather=true". But the tool signature only includes params: {latitude?,longitude?}. It doesn't mention other optional parameters like hourly etc. However maybe we can pass additional keys as part of params dictionary if allowed. Let's check the definition: In the tool description, under params there are fields: latitude, longitude, elevation. No others. So cannot specify extra param via this tool. That might limit us. But perhaps we could still get some data using default behavior which may return forecast but not necessarily current. Actually open-meteo API returns daily/hourly forecasts unless specifying "current_weather=true".

But since our tool does not allow passing arbitrary params beyond those defined, we can't set current_weather flag. Maybe we can rely on default output containing "hourly" data including temperatures at different times. Or we can just call the API without specifying anything else. We'll see what the result looks like.

Alternatively, we could manually construct the full URL ourselves inside the tool invocation. The tool expects url parameter separately. We can embed all query parameters into the URL itself. Yes! Because the tool has separate arguments: url, headers, timeout, params, etc. The params argument will add them automatically. But we can also encode them directly in the URL. But better to use params dict.

However, the params dict only accepts latitude, longitude, elevation. So we can't pass "current_weather=true". But we can put it in the URL path after '?', e.g., "?latitude=...&longitude=..." plus "&current_weather=true"? Not sure if the tool allows adding custom query strings outside of params. Usually the library would combine base URL + '?' + encoded params. Additional ones not listed won't appear. Unless we hack by putting entire query string in the URL itself. Eg: url="https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=40.7128&longitude=-74.0060&current_weather=true"

Yes, that's possible because the tool uses the given URL exactly. Then the params object may override or merge? Typically they'd append params onto the URL. But if we already include query string in URL, they might double-add? Might cause duplication. Safer to supply empty params {} and build everything into URL.

Thus let's do:

URL: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=40.7128&longitude=-74.0060&current_weather=true"

Set headers default. Use default values.

We'll then parse JSON returned. Should contain "current_weather":{temperature,...}

Let's proceed.
